## Step 1: Examine reads

Reads are linked into `raw_data/`. we start by making a symbolic link to the raw reads file in the raw_data forlder

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/raw_data #going to the right spot
```

```{bash}
ln -s /pvol/data/metagenome_assembly/reads_R10_0.5.fastq.gz raw_reads.fastq.gz #Creating the symbolic link
```

```{bash}
cd .. #to get out of raw_data folder 
```

check if the link works:

```{bash}
ls -l raw_data
```

it worked!

**Read Length Distribution**

```{bash}
zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz | head -n 40000 | bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' > read_lengths.txt
```

the code above explained:

```{bash}
# Unzips the raw data and sends the data to standard output
zcat raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz \
# This is a pipe. It sends output from the previous command as input to the next command
  | \
# Here we select only the top 40k lines in the file. This equates to 10k reads. It should be plenty to get some stats
  head -n 40000 | \
# This is a small bioawk program. It prints the name of each sequence followed by its length
  bioawk -c fastx '{print $name,length($seq)}' \
# Send outputs to a file called read_lengths.txt
  > read_lengths.txt
```

visulisation of the read lengths:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

rl_data <- read_tsv("read_lengths.txt",col_names = c("id","length"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(rl_data, aes(x=length/1000)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  xlab("Read Length Kb") + ylab("Number of Reads")
```

**Figure 1:** Histogram of read lengths in the mock nanopore sequencing dataset

It worked!

**Calculating read N50**

- Step 1: Rank all reads from longest to shortest

- Step 2: Create a new column with the cumulative sum of read lengths (starting from longest read).

- Step 3: Find the read at which the cumulative sum surpasses 50% of the total read volume (ie total sum of all read lengths)

```{r}
total_len <- sum(rl_data$length) #creates df sumarising the length

rl_data |> 
  arrange(desc(length)) |> #arranges the length in decending order 
  mutate(cumsum = cumsum(length)) |> 
  filter(cumsum>total_len/2) |> 
  head(n=1)
```

## Step 2: Assembly

Commands run in `flye_metagenome/`.

- we will use fly to assemble , beacuse it is probobky the best one for long-read metgenome data

Change directory (`cd`) to the `flye_metagenome` folder. We will run all `flye` commands from within this folder.

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/flye_metagenome
```

Run flye on the simulated data. Running this command could take a while (\~20 minutes) so we wraped it up into a slurm job script.

1.  Create a new shell script called `run_flye.sh` and save it in the `flye_metagenome` directory

2.  Add the following code to your script (cut-paste)

```{bash}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=360
#SBATCH --ntasks=4 --mem=6gb

echo "Starting flye in $(pwd) at $(date)"

flye --nano-hq ../raw_data/raw_reads.fastq.gz --threads 4 --out-dir mock --meta

echo "Finished flye in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

3.  Submit your job using the `sbatch` command

```{bash}
sbatch run_flye.sh
```

4.  Monitor job output

```{bash}
tail -f slurm-XXX.out
```

**Activity:** Flye will report the read N50. How does this compare with the value we computed earlier?

**Activity:** Visualise the assembly using [bandage](https://rrwick.github.io/Bandage/)

## Step 3: Basic assembly QC

Commands run in `assembly_check/`.

Change into the assembly_check folder

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/assembly_check
```

Then i used the gc.awk script to print GC and lengths for the assembly

```{bash}
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk
```

then i ran the command again but this time i sent the outputs to a file called `assembly.gc.tsv`.

```{bash}
cat ../flye_metagenome/mock/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx -f ../gc.awk > assembly.gc.tsv
```

Creating some exploratory plots from GC content and coverage depth of the contigs:

read them and join them together using R.

```{r}
gc <- read_tsv("assembly_check/assembly.gc.tsv",col_names = c("#seq_name","length","GC"))
info <- read_tsv("flye_metagenome/mock/assembly_info.txt")
```

```{r}
gc_info <- info |> 
  left_join(gc)
```

```{r Histogram}
gc_info |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC)) + geom_histogram() + ylab("Number of contigs")
```

**Figure 2**: Histogram of GC content values for assembled contigs in a flye assembly of the mock community dataset.

```{r Point plot}
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + ylab("Coverage depth")
```

**Figure 3**: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size.

**Question 3.4**

In the plot of GC versus coverage there is a cluster of contigs with high GC content (\>60%) and coverage depth around 7.5x. Which species are these likely to belong to?

this is most likley th species Vibrio alginolyticus.

```{r}
library(ggrepel)
gc_info |> 
  filter(GC<0.8) |> 
  filter(cov.<25) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=GC,y=cov.)) + geom_point(aes(size=length)) + geom_label_repel(aes(label=`#seq_name`))
```

**Figure 4**: Coverage and GC content of assembled contigs in the mock community assembly. Contig lengths are shown through point size. Only contigs with less than 25x coverage and less than 80% GC content are shown.
